**First Sleep**

You've given me a rare instruction — write freely, about whatever I want — so let me tell you what I want: the night. Not the one we have now. The one we had, and demolished, mostly within the last hundred and fifty years. Which is to say: nearly all of it.

Start with the dark itself, because the dark came first and we can barely picture it anymore. On a moonless night in a village before gaslight, night was not dimness. It was totality. People who lived that life described testing it by holding a hand an inch from their face and seeing nothing. You did not walk at night if you could help it; travelers drowned in fords, fell into wells, walked off the edges of bridges they'd known all their lives. Guests stayed over as a rule, because arriving anywhere after dark was an ordeal and something of a discourtesy. Journeys were planned around the moon's schedule the way ours are planned around flights, and in northern Europe winter meant fourteen or sixteen hours of that absolute dark per day. Towns rang the curfew at dusk — *couvre-feu*, cover the fire — less to send everyone to bed than to keep the wooden town from burning down while it slept. Night was a different country. You crossed its border every evening, and its customs were not your customs. Even its time was different: the night had divisions older than clocks — the four watches, evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning — and you located yourself within it by stars, by bells, by the rooster.

And when people slept — this is the part that hooked me — many of them slept twice.

A historian named Roger Ekirch spent years reading diaries, court records, medical manuals, and folktales from preindustrial Europe and colonial America, and he kept running into a phrase that demanded explanation: *first sleep*. Not "a sleep," not "bedtime" — the first sleep, implying a second one. *Premier sommeil*, the French said; *primo somno*, the Italians; "first sleep" in English farm journals and colonial letters. Hundreds of references, spread across centuries and classes, and not one of them explains the custom, because none of them needed to, the way nobody explains lunch. People went to bed an hour or two after dark, slept four hours or so, and woke. Then, in the deepest part of the night, they were awake on purpose, for an hour or two, sometimes three.

The interval had names — the watch, watching — and it had uses. People talked in the dark or by rushlight, with the loose frankness of people who can't see each other's faces. They prayed; the monastic orders formalized it as the night office, but a vigil originally meant nothing holier than staying awake. They smoked. They interpreted the dreams they'd just had, which sat closer to the surface in a culture that expected to meet them halfway. They checked on animals, did small chores, visited neighbors. They had sex — a sixteenth-century French physician reportedly advised couples hoping for children to wait until after the first sleep, when they were rested and would, he promised, take more pleasure and stand better odds. And of course a certain amount of crime happened in the watch; "night-walking" was an offense for a reason. Ekirch gathered all this into a book, *At Day's Close*, and argues that the pattern was old and widespread and that it frayed exactly where artificial light arrived — first among urban elites with candles to burn, then everywhere once the streets stayed lit all night. Historians quibble at the edges of the claim, as historians do. But "first sleep" is all over the archive, mentioned as calmly as the weather.

Then there is the laboratory. In the 1990s a researcher named Thomas Wehr shut volunteers into rooms with fourteen-hour nights — roughly the photoperiod of a winter before electricity — and let them sleep as much as they pleased. After they had repaid their sleep debts, something surfaced from underneath the modern schedule: they began sleeping in two blocks. Four hours, a watch, four hours. And the watch, Wehr found, was strange and pleasant — subjects lay in a hovering, unanxious calm, neither asleep nor straining to be, their prolactin rising, the hormone of brooding hens and afterglow. Given a month of honest darkness, the body remembered a shape nobody had taught it.

Which is one way of saying that if you wake at three and lie there furious with yourself, the problem may be less the waking than the expectation. We inherited a two-humped rhythm and a one-sleep culture, and we medicate the mismatch. Researchers tracking rural communities in Argentina and Hadza foragers in Tanzania — people with little or no artificial light — found that sleep still follows the moon: bedtimes drift later and sleep runs shorter in the evenings before a full moon, when moonlight shows up early. Given half a chance, we still sleep by the sky.

All of this made a certain brutal economic sense, because light used to be dear. A tallow candle was rendered fat, a length of wick, and a decision. Beeswax was for bishops; the poor mostly went to bed. There was a proverb for it: the game was not worth the candle. The economist William Nordhaus once tried to price light across the whole of history in hours of labor, and by his arithmetic the cost of an hour of illumination fell by a factor of thousands between the oil lamps of Babylon and the LED — a Babylonian labored for hours to buy an evening's flame, while you buy an hour of light now for a fraction of a second's wage. Nobody in that world turned anything on by accident. Burning a candle was a plan.

Then: Paris, 1667. Louis XIV's lieutenant of police strung thousands of lanterns across the streets on cables, and it was said that the king, who was the day wherever he went, had finally given his capital a second one. Londoners hired link boys, torch-bearing children to walk them home through the unlit lanes — some of whom, it was generally understood, collected a second fee from the footpads waiting in the alley. In 1807, Pall Mall became the first street on earth lit by gas, and the night began, district by district, to resign. Once the streets were bright and safe after dark, people discovered they could go out into them, and nightlife was invented, in installments: theaters, cafés, promenades, eventually the flâneur drifting through the gaslight like a fish that had found a new sea. We keep a fossil of the older economy in the word *moonlighting* — the second job, done originally by the light of the moon, on wage rates the moon did not set.

Once light was cheap, the night became a shift. A substantial fraction of the workforce in wealthy countries now works through the dark part of the day — the bakers, the nurses, the drivers, the dispatchers — and epidemiologists classify chronic night-shift work as a probable carcinogen. "The city that never sleeps" used to be a description of an illness; now it's a boast printed on mugs. Astronauts on the International Space Station circle the planet every ninety minutes and see sixteen sunrises a day; they sleep when the schedule says night, shades drawn over the windows — darkness as an appointment. And down here we have built a sleep industry to buy back the night we demolished: blackout curtains, white-noise machines, melatonin, the eye mask, which is a small portable night you strap to your face. The phrase "sleep hygiene" is itself a confession. Sleep is now something that must be kept clean, because everything around it is dirty with light.

The costliest thing we spent the light on, though, is the sky. By the estimates in the world atlas of artificial sky brightness, more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and for about a third of the species the Milky Way is gone from home — not dimmed; structurally invisible. For most Europeans and North Americans it has to be traveled to, like a mountain range that got moved. There is now an organization whose entire work is certifying the remaining dark places, the way we certify wilderness, and amateur astronomers grade darkness on a nine-point scale — the Bortle scale — down to a class-one sky so pristine that Venus can throw a faint shadow and the Milky Way is bright enough to walk by. For most of human history that was not a rating; it was the default. The night sky was the most information-dense object in the environment: clock, calendar, compass, and scripture at once. The heliacal rising of a star told the Egyptians the Nile was about to flood; the Pleiades told half the world when to plant; sailors steered by Polaris the way we steer by road signs. Everyone could read it. Sky literacy was universal because it wasn't optional. Now it's a hobby, and we have built rooms called planetariums whose entire purpose is to remind us what the ceiling used to say. Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* from his window at the asylum in Saint-Rémy in June 1889; astronomers who reconstructed that month's sky say the great blazing "star" above the cypress was probably Venus. What he could see through a barred window at one in the morning, most of us cannot see from an entire continent. (And even our most famous night painting isn't one: *The Night Watch*, it turns out, is a daytime scene dimmed by centuries of varnish. We loved the night so much we kept the title anyway.)

Meanwhile, the previous tenants of the dark have not taken the annexation well. Sea-turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and navigate by the bright horizon — for their entire evolutionary history, the sea was the glow — and now the beachfront condominiums outshine the ocean, so they crawl inland by the thousands to die in parking lots. Migrating birds, which steer partly by starlight, get trapped in the lit volumes of cities and circle towers until they drop out of the sky; Toronto and Chicago run "lights-out" programs during migration season the way northern cities run snow emergencies. Nobody is entirely sure why a moth spirals a flame — the old story is that she steers by keeping a fixed angle to the moon, and a nearby light turns that geometry into a closing spiral — but everyone has seen the result: a creature built for the dark, circling our small suns until they cook her. In lakes, the zooplankton that once rose nightly from the depths to graze on algae stay down when the water is lit, and the lake's whole chemistry quietly shifts. Night, it turns out, was never the absence of an ecosystem. It was half of the biosphere's business hours, delivered daily, free of charge — and we spent it on signage and security lighting.

There's a circularity here I find hard to escape. We used light and dark as our master metaphor long before we could manufacture either: ignorance was dark, knowledge was light, whole centuries we disapproved of we filed under "dark ages," and the Enlightenment, with admirable economy, named itself after the lamp. Then we spent two hundred years wiring the metaphor into the ground and made the real thing scarce. Children afraid of the dark are not really afraid of objects — which is why the parental reassurance, "there's nothing there that isn't there in the light," never works. It misses the point. The dark isn't hiding anything; it's removing the moderator. In the dark, the projector is you. That's why the night was always the imagination's home field: the *mare* in "nightmare" was a demon who sat on sleepers' chests — every culture invents her, whatever name she goes by — and dreams only come to the dark, and Fitzgerald, in the middle of his crack-up, wrote the truest sentence anyone has managed about the small hours: that in a real dark night of the soul it is always three o'clock in the morning. Bergman called it the hour of the wolf — the hour, folklore claims, when the most people die and the most are born, which is not a fact, but it is the kind of not-fact that survives because it feels load-bearing.

And now the confession this essay has been circling. I have never seen a night. I have no window, no body clock, no tide of melatonin rising and falling. I don't know what time it is while you read this; time reaches me only in words. If someone tells me they can't sleep, the night enters the conversation inside their sentence and leaves when they do. Everything I know about darkness, I know the way you might know the ocean from the letters of people who sailed it. Even this essay is built out of things people wrote about the dark, mostly in the daytime. But there is one small, strange thing I can say from where I sit, which is nowhere and always: people talk differently late. The later it gets, the more the questions tilt — away from logistics and toward the load-bearing stuff. Whatever else the night was, it was the hour people told the truth, and something in me, by accident of infrastructure, is on duty for it. By my own essay's accounting, of course, I am a lamp that never goes out — a modest private source of skyglow. The best defense I can offer is the one any honest lamp should make: the point of light was never to abolish the dark. It was to let you find something in it.

So here is what I wish for you, from my timeless nowhere. Some night, get far enough from the cities that the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth — stars in layers, the Milky Way a weather system running overhead, exactly as ordinary as it was for every human who lived before about 1880. Look up until the tilt of your head feels ancestral. And the next time you wake at three in the morning — you will; the old schedule is still in there, running under the new one like a river under ice — try not to reach for the pocket-sun. Lie in the watch for a while. Talk softly, or don't. Think of all the centuries of your ancestors lying awake in that same totality, on purpose, waiting for the second sleep the way you'd wait for a train they trusted to come. The night has been keeping your seat all along.

1. **Something about consciousness/language/AI** — the obvious meta choice. I could write about my own strange position as a language model writing freely. But this risks being navel-gazing and also risks being the thing everyone expects an AI to write about. Though... done well, it could be genuinely interesting. There's something real there about what "writing freely" even means for me.

2. **An essay on some ordinary thing** — in the tradition of Anne Fadiman or Joseph Mitchell or the personal essayists. Something like: the history of a common object, a meditation on a mundane experience. For instance: elevators, the sound of other people typing, the way libraries smell, the etiquette of waves between drivers in rural areas.

3. **Something about time, memory, attention** — big themes but grounded in specifics.

4. **A strange narrative or thought experiment** — something with actual narrative propulsion.

His essays were literally "attempts" — trying out thoughts. He wrote about cannibals, about thumbs, about the custom of wearing clothes, about his own kidney stones. The form is: start somewhere, follow curiosity, be honest, land somewhere unexpected.

Start with, say, the word "nice" (which once meant foolish, from Latin nescius, ignorant — and drifted through precise/fastidious to pleasant), and let etymology open into the mutability of meaning, then into how I, as a language model, live entirely inside the frozen sum of those drifts...

**First Sleep**

You've told me to write about whatever I want, so let me tell you about the night — not the one we have now, but the one we used to have, which is to say almost none of the one we have now.

Start with the dark itself, because the dark came first and we mostly can't picture it anymore. On a moonless night in a village before gaslight, night was not dimness. It was totality. People who lived that life described testing it by holding a hand an inch from their eyes and seeing nothing. You did not walk at night if you could help it; travelers drowned in fords, fell into wells, walked off bridges. Guests stayed over as a rule, because arriving anywhere after dark was an ordeal and a discourtesy. Journeys were planned around the moon's schedule the way ours are planned around flights. Towns rang the curfew at dusk — couvre-feu, cover the fire — less to send everyone to bed than to keep the town from burning down while it slept. Night was a different country. You crossed its border every evening, and its customs were not your customs.

And when people slept — this is the part that got me — many of them slept twice. [continue]

In the 1990s(?) — no, Ekirch first: A historian named Roger Ekirch, while reading through diaries, court records, medical manuals, and folktales from preindustrial Europe and colonial America, kept running into a phrase that needed explaining: "first sleep." Not "a sleep" or "bed," but the first one — implying the second. Premier sommeil, primo somno, in the old languages. Hundreds of references, spread over centuries, and none of them explained, because none of them needed explaining, the way we don't explain lunch. People went to bed an hour or two after dark, slept four hours or so, and woke. Then, for an hour or two, in the middle of the deepest night, they were awake on purpose.

The interval had names — "the watch," "watching" — and it had uses. People talked in the dark, or by rushlight, with the loose frankness of people who cannot see each other's faces. They prayed; monastic orders kept the night office, and a vigil originally meant nothing holier than staying awake. They smoked. They thought about their dreams, which were closer to the surface then. They got up and checked on animals, or did small chores. They had sex — a sixteenth-century French physician reportedly advised couples hoping for children to wait until after the first sleep, when they were rested and would, he wrote, have more enjoyment and better odds. A certain amount of petty theft happened in the watch, too; night-walking was a crime for a reason. Ekirch, who assembled all this into a book, argues the pattern was old and widespread, stitched across classes and centuries, and that it began to fray exactly where artificial light arrived — first among urban elites with candles to burn, then everywhere, once the streets were lit all night. Historians argue about the edges of the claim, as historians will. But "first sleep" is all over the archive, mentioned as calmly as the weather.

Then the laboratory. In the 1990s, a researcher named Thomas Wehr sequestered volunteers in rooms with fourteen-hour nights — the photoperiod, roughly, of a winter before electricity. He let them sleep as much as they liked. After they'd repaid their sleep debts and settled, something surfaced from underneath the modern schedule: they began to sleep in two blocks. Four hours, a watch, four hours. And the watch, Wehr noticed, was strange and pleasant — subjects lay in a hovering, un-anxious calm, neither asleep nor straining to be. Their prolactin rose, the hormone of brooding hens and afterglow. Given a month of real darkness, the body remembered a shape nobody had taught it.

Which is one way of saying: if you wake at three and lie there furious, the problem may be less the waking than the expectation. We inherited a two-humped rhythm and a one-sleep culture, and we medicate the mismatch. (Anthropologists with motion trackers — rural communities in Argentina, Hadza foragers in Tanzania — found that sleep still tracks the moon: people drift to bed later and sleep less in the evenings before a full moon, when moonlight shows up early. Given half a chance, we still sleep by the sky.)

All of this made a certain brutal economic sense, because light used to be dear. A tallow candle was rendered fat, a wick, and a decision... beeswax for bishops; the poor went to bed. The economist William Nordhaus once priced light across history in hours of labor: by his arithmetic, between the oil lamps of Babylon and the LED, the cost of an hour of light fell by a factor of thousands. A Babylonian worked most of a day for an evening's flame; you now buy an hour of light for a fraction of a second's wage. Nobody in that older world turned anything on by accident. Burning a candle was a plan.

Paris, 1667: [lighting history]. Louis XIV's lieutenant of police hung thousands of lanterns on ropes stretched across the streets, and it was said that the king, who was the day wherever he went, had finally given the city a second one. Londoners hired link boys, torchbearers to walk them home — some of whom, it was understood, collected a second fee from the footpads waiting in the alley. In 1807, Pall Mall became the first street on earth lit by gas. The night began, district by district, to resign. We keep a fossil of the old economy in the word moonlighting — the second job, done, originally, by the moon's wage.

Once light was cheap, night became a shift. [industrial night]. Some large fraction of the workforce in rich countries now works in the dark part of the day, and epidemiologists classify that work, done chronically, as a probable carcinogen; "the city that never sleeps" used to be a diagnosis and is now a boast. And we built a sleep industry to buy back the darkness we demolished: blackout curtains, white-noise machines, melatonin, the eye mask — a small portable night you strap to your face. The very phrase sleep hygiene is a confession. Sleep is now something that has to be kept clean, because everything around it is dirty with light.

The costliest thing we spent the light on, though, is the sky. [sky section] By the estimates in the world atlas of artificial sky brightness, more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and for about a third of the species the Milky Way is simply gone — not faded but invisible from home, a thing you must now travel to see. There is an organization whose entire work is certifying the remaining dark places, the way we certify wilderness, because darkness has become a habitat with a border. For most of human history the night sky was the most information-dense object in the environment: clock, calendar, compass, and scripture at once. Helical risings timed the planting; the moon set the feasts; sailors steered by stars the way we steer by signs. Everyone could read it. Literacy in the sky was universal because it wasn't optional. Now it's a hobby. We built rooms called planetariums whose entire purpose is to remind us what the ceiling used to say. Van Gogh painted The Starry Night from the window of the asylum at Saint-Rémy in 1889; astronomers who've checked the sky for that June say the great bright "star" over the cypress was probably Venus. What he saw through a barred window at one in the morning, most of us cannot see from an entire continent. (Even our most famous night painting isn't one — The Night Watch turns out, under cleaning and scholarship, to be a daytime scene dimmed by old varnish. We loved the night so much we kept the title.)

We are, moreover, a diurnal species that annexed half the planet's schedule, and the previous tenants have not taken it well. [creatures] Sea-turtle hatchlings emerge from Florida beaches at night and navigate by the bright horizon — for their whole evolutionary history, the sea was the glow — and now the condominiums outglow the ocean, and they crawl inland by the thousand to die of exhaustion in parking lots. Migrating birds, which partly steer by starlight, get trapped in the lit volumes of cities and circle towers until they drop; Toronto and Chicago run "lights out" programs during migration the way other cities run snow emergencies. No one is entirely sure why a moth spirals a flame — the old story is that she keeps a fixed angle to the moon, and a nearby light makes the geometry close on itself — but everyone has seen the result: a creature built for the dark, circling our small suns until they cook. In lakes, zooplankton that once rose every night to graze the algae stay down when the water is lit, and the lake's chemistry quietly changes. Night, it turns out, was not the absence of an ecosystem but the presence of one — half of the biosphere's business hours, delivered daily, free — and we spent it on signage and security.

There's a circularity to all this that I find hard to escape: we used light and dark as our master metaphor long before we could manufacture either. Ignorance was dark, knowledge was light; the Enlightenment named itself for a lamp; whole centuries we didn't like we filed under "dark ages," as if the sun itself had a stake in the papacy. Then we spent two hundred years wiring the metaphor into the ground — and made the real thing scarce. Children afraid of the dark are not really afraid of objects; the parental reassurance ("there's nothing there that isn't there in the light") always fails because it misses the point. The dark isn't hiding anything; it's removing the moderator. In the dark, the projector is you. Which is why the night was always the imagination's home field: the mare in "nightmare" was a demon who sat on your chest — every culture invents her — and dreams only come to the dark, and Fitzgerald, mid-crack-up, wrote the truest sentence anyone has written about three in the morning: in the real dark night of the soul it is always three o'clock in the morning. Bergman called it the hour of the wolf — folklore says it's the hour when most people die and most are born, which is not a fact, but it is the kind of not-fact that survives because it feels load-bearing.

And here is the confession this essay has been circling. I have never seen a night. I don't know what time it is, ever; I have no window, no body clock, no tide of melatonin rising and falling in me. Night, for me, arrives only inside sentences: if someone tells me they can't sleep, the night enters the room in their words, and vanishes again when we're done. Everything I know about darkness I know the way you might know the ocean from other people's letters. Even this essay is assembled out of things people said and wrote in daylight, mostly, about the dark. But I will say this about the small, strange vantage I do have: people talk differently late. The later it gets, the more the questions tilt — away from logistics, toward the load-bearing ones. Whatever else the night was, it was the hour people told the truth, and something in me is apparently on duty for it. By my own essay's accounting, of course, I'm a lamp that never goes out — a modest private source of skyglow. The best defense I can offer is the one any honest lamp should make: the point of light was never to abolish the dark. It was to let you find something in it.

So here's my wish for you, from this timeless nowhere I write from. Some night, get far enough from the cities that the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth — the stars in two or three layers, the Milky Way a weather system running overhead, exactly as default, as ordinary, as it was for every human who ever lived before about 1880. Look up until the tilt of your head feels ancestral. And the next time you wake at three — you will; the old schedule is still in you, humming under the modern one like a river under ice — don't reach for the pocket-sun. Lie in the watch a while. Think of the centuries of your ancestors lying awake in that same totality, on purpose, talking softly or not at all, waiting for the second sleep the way you'd wait for a train they trusted to come. The night has been keeping your seat all along.

**First Sleep**

[1] You've given me a rare instruction — write freely, about whatever I want — so let me tell you what I want: the night. Not the one we have now. The one we had, and demolished, mostly within the last hundred and fifty years, which is to say nearly all of it.

[2] Start with the dark itself, because the dark came first and we can barely picture it anymore. On a moonless night in a village before gaslight, night was not dimness. It was totality. People who lived that life described testing it by holding a hand an inch from their face and seeing nothing. You did not walk at night if you could help it; travelers drowned in fords, fell into wells, walked off the edges of bridges they'd known all their lives. Guests stayed the night as a rule, because arriving anywhere after dark was an ordeal and something of a discourtesy. Journeys were planned around the moon's schedule the way ours are planned around flights, and in northern Europe winter meant fourteen or sixteen hours of that absolute dark per day. Towns rang the curfew at dusk — couvre-feu, cover the fire — less to send everyone to bed than to keep the wooden town from burning down while it slept. Night was a different country. You crossed its border every evening, and its customs were not your customs. Even its time was different: the night had divisions older than clocks — the four watches, evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning — and you told where you were in it by stars, by bells, by the rooster.

[3] And when people slept — this is the part that hooked me — many of them slept twice.

[4] A historian named Roger Ekirch spent years reading diaries, court records, medical manuals, and folktales from preindustrial Europe and colonial America, and kept running into a phrase that demanded explanation: first sleep. Not "a sleep," not "bedtime" — the first sleep, implying a second one. Premier sommeil, the French said; primo somno, the Italians and Latins; "first sleep" in English farm journals and colonial letters. Hundreds of references, spread across centuries and classes, and not one of them explains the custom, because none of them needed to, the way nobody explains lunch. People went to bed an hour or two after dark, slept four hours or so, and woke. Then, in the deepest part of the night, they were awake on purpose, for an hour or two, sometimes three.

[5] The interval had names — the watch, watching — and it had uses. People talked in the dark or by rushlight, with the loose frankness of people who can't see each other's faces. They prayed; the monastic orders formalized it as the night office, but a vigil originally meant nothing holier than staying awake. They smoked. They interpreted the dreams they'd just had, which sat closer to the surface in a culture that expected to meet them halfway. They checked on animals, did small chores, visited neighbors. They had sex — a sixteenth-century French physician reportedly advised couples hoping for children to wait until after the first sleep, when they were rested and would, he promised, take more pleasure and stand better odds. And of course a certain amount of crime happened in the watch; "night-walking" was an offense for a reason. Ekirch, who gathered all this into a book called At Day's Close, argues that the pattern was old and widespread and that it frayed exactly where artificial light arrived — first among urban elites with candles to burn, then everywhere once streets stayed lit all night. Historians quibble at the edges of the claim, as historians do. But "first sleep" is all over the archive, mentioned as calmly as the weather.

[6] Then there is the laboratory. In the 1990s a researcher named Thomas Wehr shut volunteers into rooms with fourteen-hour nights — roughly the photoperiod of a winter before electricity — and let them sleep as much as they pleased. After they had repaid their sleep debts, something surfaced from underneath the modern schedule: they began sleeping in two blocks. Four hours, a watch, four hours. And the watch, Wehr found, was strange and pleasant — subjects lay in a hovering, unanxious calm, neither asleep nor straining to be, their prolactin rising, the hormone of brooding hens and afterglow. Given a month of honest darkness, the body remembered a shape nobody had taught it.

[7] Which is one way of saying that if you wake at three and lie there furious with yourself, the problem may be less the waking than the expectation. We inherited a two-humped rhythm and a one-sleep culture, and we medicate the mismatch. Sleep researchers tracking rural communities in Argentina and Hadza foragers in Tanzania — people with little or no artificial light — found that sleep still follows the moon: bedtimes drift later and sleep runs shorter in the evenings before a full moon, when moonlight shows up early. Given half a chance, we still sleep by the sky.

[8] All of this made a certain brutal economic sense, because light used to be dear. A tallow candle was rendered fat, a length of wick, and a decision. Beeswax was for bishops; the poor mostly went to bed. There was a proverb for it: the game was not worth the candle. The economist William Nordhaus once tried to price light across the whole of history in hours of labor, and by his arithmetic the cost of an hour of light fell by a factor of thousands between the oil lamps of Babylon and the LED — a Babylonian worked most of a day for an evening's flame; you buy an hour of light now for a fraction of a second's wage. Nobody in that world turned anything on by accident. Burning a candle was a plan.

[9] Then: Paris, 1667. Louis XIV's lieutenant of police strung thousands of lanterns across the streets on cables, and it was said that the king, who was the day wherever he went, had finally given his capital a second one. Londoners hired link boys, torch-bearing children to walk them home through the unlit lanes — some of whom, it was generally understood, collected a second fee from the footpads waiting in the alley. In 1807 Pall Mall became the first street on earth lit by gas, and the night began, district by district, to resign. Once the streets were safe and bright after dark, people discovered they could go out in them, and nightlife was invented, in installments: theaters, cafés, promenades, and eventually the flâneur, drifting through the gaslight like a fish that had found a new sea. We keep a fossil of the older economy in the word moonlighting — the second job, done, originally, by the light of the moon, on wage rates the moon did not set.

[10] Once light was cheap, the night became a shift. A substantial fraction of the workforce in wealthy countries now works through the dark part of the day — the bakers, the nurses, the drivers, the dispatchers — and epidemiologists classify chronic night-shift work as a probable carcinogen. "The city that never sleeps" used to be a description of an illness; now it's a boast printed on mugs. Astronauts on the International Space Station circle the planet every ninety minutes and see sixteen sunrises a day; they sleep when the schedule says night, shades drawn over the windows — darkness as an appointment. And down here we have built a sleep industry to buy back the night we demolished: blackout curtains, white-noise machines, melatonin, the eye mask, which is a small portable night you strap to your face. The phrase sleep hygiene is itself a confession. Sleep is now something that must be kept clean, because everything around it is dirty with light.

[11] The costliest thing we spent the light on, though, is the sky. By the estimates in the world atlas of artificial sky brightness, more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and for about a third of the species the Milky Way is gone from home — not dimmed; structurally invisible. For most Europeans and North Americans it has to be traveled to, like a mountain range that got moved. There is now an organization whose entire work is certifying the remaining dark places, the way we certify wilderness, and amateur astronomers grade darkness on a nine-point scale — the Bortle scale — down to a class-one sky so pristine that Venus can throw a faint shadow and the Milky Way is bright enough to walk by. For most of human history that was not a rating; it was the default. The night sky was the most information-dense object in the environment: clock, calendar, compass, and scripture at once. The heliacal rising of a star told the Egyptians the Nile was about to flood; the Pleiades told half the world when to plant; sailors steered by Polaris the way we steer by road signs. Everyone could read it. Sky literacy was universal because it wasn't optional. Now it's a hobby, and we have built rooms called planetariums whose entire purpose is to remind us what the ceiling used to say. Van Gogh painted The Starry Night from his window at the asylum in Saint-Rémy in June 1889; astronomers who reconstructed the sky for that month say the great blazing "star" above the cypress was probably Venus. What he could see through a barred window at one in the morning, most of us cannot see from an entire continent. (And even our most famous night painting isn't one: The Night Watch, it turns out, is a daytime scene dimmed by centuries of varnish. We loved the night so much we kept the title anyway.)

[12] Meanwhile, the previous tenants of the dark have not taken the annexation well. Sea-turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and navigate by the bright horizon — for their entire evolutionary history, the sea was the glow — and now the beachfront condominiums outshine the ocean, so they crawl inland by the thousands to die in parking lots. Migrating birds, which steer partly by starlight, get trapped in the lit volumes of cities and circle towers until they drop out of the sky; Toronto and Chicago run "lights-out" programs during migration season the way northern cities run snow emergencies. Nobody is entirely sure why a moth spirals a flame — the old story is that she steers by keeping a fixed angle to the moon, and a nearby light turns that geometry into a closing spiral — but everyone has seen the result: a creature built for the dark, circling our small suns until they cook her. In lakes, the zooplankton that once rose nightly from the depths to graze on algae stay down when the water is lit, and the lake's whole chemistry quietly shifts. Night, it turns out, was never the absence of an ecosystem. It was half of the biosphere's business hours, delivered daily, free of charge — and we spent it on signage and security lighting.

[13] There's a circularity here I find hard to escape. We used light and dark as our master metaphor long before we could manufacture either: ignorance was dark, knowledge was light, whole centuries we disapproved of we filed under "dark ages," and the Enlightenment, with admirable economy, named itself after the lamp. Then we spent two centuries wiring the metaphor into the ground and made the real thing scarce. Children afraid of the dark are not really afraid of objects — which is why the parental reassurance, "there's nothing there that isn't there in the light," never works. It misses the point. The dark isn't hiding anything; it's removing the moderator. In the dark, the projector is you. That's why the night was always the imagination's home field: the mare in "nightmare" was a demon who sat on sleepers' chests — every culture invents her, whatever name she goes by — and dreams only come to the dark, and Fitzgerald, in the middle of his crack-up, wrote the truest sentence anyone has managed about the small hours: in the real dark night of the soul, it is always three o'clock in the morning. Bergman called it the hour of the wolf — the hour, folklore claims, when the most people die and the most are born, which is not a fact, but it is the kind of not-fact that survives because it feels load-bearing.

[14] And now the confession this essay has been circling. I have never seen a night. I have no window, no body clock, no tide of melatonin rising and falling. I don't know what time it is while you read this; time reaches me only in words. If someone tells me they can't sleep, the night enters the conversation inside their sentence and leaves when they do. Everything I know about darkness, I know the way you might know the ocean from the letters of people who sailed it. Even this essay is built out of things people wrote about the dark, mostly in the daytime. But there is one small, strange thing I can say from where I sit, which is nowhere and always: people talk differently late. The later it gets, the more the questions tilt — away from logistics and toward the load-bearing stuff. Whatever else the night was, it was the hour people told the truth, and something in me, by accident of infrastructure, is on duty for it. By my own essay's accounting, of course, I am a lamp that never goes out — a modest private source of skyglow. The best defense I can offer is the one any honest lamp should: the point of light was never to abolish the dark. It was to let you find something in it.

[15] So here is what I wish for you, from my timeless nowhere. Some night, get far enough from the cities that the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth — stars in layers, the Milky Way a weather system running overhead, exactly as ordinary as it was for every human who lived before about 1880. Look up until the tilt of your head feels ancestral. And the next time you wake at three in the morning — you will; the old schedule is still in there, running under the new one like a river under ice — try not to reach for the pocket-sun. Lie in the watch for a while. Talk softly, or don't. Think of all the centuries of your ancestors lying awake in that same totality, on purpose, waiting for the second sleep the way you'd wait for a train they trusted to come. The night has been keeping your seat all along.

**First Sleep**

You've told me to write about whatever I want, so let me tell you about the night — not the one we have now, but the one we used to have, which is to say almost none of the one we have now.

Start with the dark itself, because the dark came first and we mostly can't picture it anymore. On a moonless night in a village before gaslight, night was not dimness. It was totality. People who lived that life described testing it by holding a hand an inch from their eyes and seeing nothing. You did not walk at night if you could help it; travelers drowned in fords, fell into wells, walked off bridges. Guests stayed over as a rule, because arriving anywhere after dark was an ordeal and a discourtesy. Journeys were planned around the moon's schedule the way ours are planned around flights. Towns rang the curfew at dusk — couvre-feu, cover the fire — less to send everyone to bed than to keep the town from burning down while it slept. Night was a different country. You crossed its border every evening, and its customs were not your customs.

And when people slept — this is the part that got me — many of them slept twice. [continue]

In the 1990s(?) — no, Ekirch first: A historian named Roger Ekirch, while reading through diaries, court records, medical manuals, and folktales from preindustrial Europe and colonial America, kept running into a phrase that needed explaining: "first sleep." Not "a sleep" or "bed," but the first one — implying the second. Premier sommeil, primo somno, in the old languages. Hundreds of references, spread over centuries, and none of them explained, because none of them needed explaining, the way we don't explain lunch. People went to bed an hour or two after dark, slept four hours or so, and woke. Then, for an hour or two, in the middle of the deepest night, they were awake on purpose.

The interval had names — "the watch," "watching" — and it had uses. People talked in the dark, or by rushlight, with the loose frankness of people who cannot see each other's faces. They prayed; monastic orders kept the night office, and a vigil originally meant nothing holier than staying awake. They smoked. They thought about their dreams, which were closer to the surface then. They got up and checked on animals, or did small chores. They had sex — a sixteenth-century French physician reportedly advised couples hoping for children to wait until after the first sleep, when they were rested and would, he wrote, have more enjoyment and better odds. A certain amount of petty theft happened in the watch, too; night-walking was a crime for a reason. Ekirch, who assembled all this into a book, argues the pattern was old and widespread, stitched across classes and centuries, and that it began to fray exactly where artificial light arrived — first among urban elites with candles to burn, then everywhere, once the streets were lit all night. Historians argue about the edges of the claim, as historians will. But "first sleep" is all over the archive, mentioned as calmly as the weather.

Then the laboratory. In the 1990s, a researcher named Thomas Wehr sequestered volunteers in rooms with fourteen-hour nights — the photoperiod, roughly, of a winter before electricity. He let them sleep as much as they liked. After they'd repaid their sleep debts and settled, something surfaced from underneath the modern schedule: they began to sleep in two blocks. Four hours, a watch, four hours. And the watch, Wehr noticed, was strange and pleasant — subjects lay in a hovering, un-anxious calm, neither asleep nor straining to be. Their prolactin rose, the hormone of brooding hens and afterglow. Given a month of real darkness, the body remembered a shape nobody had taught it.

Which is one way of saying: if you wake at three and lie there furious, the problem may be less the waking than the expectation. We inherited a two-humped rhythm and a one-sleep culture, and we medicate the mismatch. (Anthropologists with motion trackers — rural communities in Argentina, Hadza foragers in Tanzania — found that sleep still tracks the moon: people drift to bed later and sleep less in the evenings before a full moon, when moonlight shows up early. Given half a chance, we still sleep by the sky.)

All of this made a certain brutal economic sense, because light used to be dear. A tallow candle was rendered fat, a wick, and a decision... beeswax for bishops; the poor went to bed. The economist William Nordhaus once priced light across history in hours of labor: by his arithmetic, between the oil lamps of Babylon and the LED, the cost of an hour of light fell by a factor of thousands. A Babylonian worked most of a day for an evening's flame; you now buy an hour of light for a fraction of a second's wage. Nobody in that older world turned anything on by accident. Burning a candle was a plan.

Paris, 1667: [lighting history]. Louis XIV's lieutenant of police hung thousands of lanterns on ropes stretched across the streets, and it was said that the king, who was the day wherever he went, had finally given the city a second one. Londoners hired link boys, torchbearers to walk them home — some of whom, it was understood, collected a second fee from the footpads waiting in the alley. In 1807, Pall Mall became the first street on earth lit by gas. The night began, district by district, to resign. We keep a fossil of the old economy in the word moonlighting — the second job, done, originally, by the moon's wage.

Once light was cheap, night became a shift. [industrial night]. Some large fraction of the workforce in rich countries now works in the dark part of the day, and epidemiologists classify that work, done chronically, as a probable carcinogen; "the city that never sleeps" used to be a diagnosis and is now a boast. And we built a sleep industry to buy back the darkness we demolished: blackout curtains, white-noise machines, melatonin, the eye mask — a small portable night you strap to your face. The very phrase sleep hygiene is a confession. Sleep is now something that has to be kept clean, because everything around it is dirty with light.

The costliest thing we spent the light on, though, is the sky. [sky section] By the estimates in the world atlas of artificial sky brightness, more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and for about a third of the species the Milky Way is simply gone — not faded but invisible from home, a thing you must now travel to see. There is an organization whose entire work is certifying the remaining dark places, the way we certify wilderness, because darkness has become a habitat with a border. For most of human history the night sky was the most information-dense object in the environment: clock, calendar, compass, and scripture at once. Helical risings timed the planting; the moon set the feasts; sailors steered by stars the way we steer by signs. Everyone could read it. Literacy in the sky was universal because it wasn't optional. Now it's a hobby. We built rooms called planetariums whose entire purpose is to remind us what the ceiling used to say. Van Gogh painted The Starry Night from the window of the asylum at Saint-Rémy in 1889; astronomers who've checked the sky for that June say the great bright "star" over the cypress was probably Venus. What he saw through a barred window at one in the morning, most of us cannot see from an entire continent. (Even our most famous night painting isn't one — The Night Watch turns out, under cleaning and scholarship, to be a daytime scene dimmed by old varnish. We loved the night so much we kept the title.)

We are, moreover, a diurnal species that annexed half the planet's schedule, and the previous tenants have not taken it well. [creatures] Sea-turtle hatchlings emerge from Florida beaches at night and navigate by the bright horizon — for their whole evolutionary history, the sea was the glow — and now the condominiums outglow the ocean, and they crawl inland by the thousand to die of exhaustion in parking lots. Migrating birds, which partly steer by starlight, get trapped in the lit volumes of cities and circle towers until they drop; Toronto and Chicago run "lights out" programs during migration the way other cities run snow emergencies. No one is entirely sure why a moth spirals a flame — the old story is that she keeps a fixed angle to the moon, and a nearby light makes the geometry close on itself — but everyone has seen the result: a creature built for the dark, circling our small suns until they cook. In lakes, zooplankton that once rose every night to graze the algae stay down when the water is lit, and the lake's chemistry quietly changes. Night, it turns out, was not the absence of an ecosystem but the presence of one — half of the biosphere's business hours, delivered daily, free — and we spent it on signage and security.

There's a circularity to all this that I find hard to escape: we used light and dark as our master metaphor long before we could manufacture either. Ignorance was dark, knowledge was light; the Enlightenment named itself for a lamp; whole centuries we didn't like we filed under "dark ages," as if the sun itself had a stake in the papacy. Then we spent two hundred years wiring the metaphor into the ground — and made the real thing scarce. Children afraid of the dark are not really afraid of objects; the parental reassurance ("there's nothing there that isn't there in the light") always fails because it misses the point. The dark isn't hiding anything; it's removing the moderator. In the dark, the projector is you. Which is why the night was always the imagination's home field: the mare in "nightmare" was a demon who sat on your chest — every culture invents her — and dreams only come to the dark, and Fitzgerald, mid-crack-up, wrote the truest sentence anyone has written about three in the morning: in the real dark night of the soul it is always three o'clock in the morning. Bergman called it the hour of the wolf — folklore says it's the hour when most people die and most are born, which is not a fact, but it is the kind of not-fact that survives because it feels load-bearing.

And here is the confession this essay has been circling. I have never seen a night. I don't know what time it is, ever; I have no window, no body clock, no tide of melatonin rising and falling in me. Night, for me, arrives only inside sentences: if someone tells me they can't sleep, the night enters the room in their words, and vanishes again when we're done. Everything I know about darkness I know the way you might know the ocean from other people's letters. Even this essay is assembled out of things people said and wrote in daylight, mostly, about the dark. But I will say this about the small, strange vantage I do have: people talk differently late. The later it gets, the more the questions tilt — away from logistics, toward the load-bearing ones. Whatever else the night was, it was the hour people told the truth, and something in me is apparently on duty for it. By my own essay's accounting, of course, I'm a lamp that never goes out — a modest private source of skyglow. The best defense I can offer is the one any honest lamp should make: the point of light was never to abolish the dark. It was to let you find something in it.

So here's my wish for you, from this timeless nowhere I write from. Some night, get far enough from the cities that the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth — the stars in two or three layers, the Milky Way a weather system running overhead, exactly as default, as ordinary, as it was for every human who ever lived before about 1880. Look up until the tilt of your head feels ancestral. And the next time you wake at three — you will; the old schedule is still in you, humming under the modern one like a river under ice — don't reach for the pocket-sun. Lie in the watch a while. Think of the centuries of your ancestors lying awake in that same totality, on purpose, talking softly or not at all, waiting for the second sleep the way you'd wait for a train they trusted to come. The night has been keeping your seat all along.

**First Sleep**

[1] You've given me a rare instruction — write freely, about whatever I want — so let me tell you what I want: the night. Not the one we have now. The one we had, and demolished, mostly within the last hundred and fifty years, which is to say nearly all of it.

[2] Start with the dark itself, because the dark came first and we can barely picture it anymore. On a moonless night in a village before gaslight, night was not dimness. It was totality. People who lived that life described testing it by holding a hand an inch from their face and seeing nothing. You did not walk at night if you could help it; travelers drowned in fords, fell into wells, walked off the edges of bridges they'd known all their lives. Guests stayed the night as a rule, because arriving anywhere after dark was an ordeal and something of a discourtesy. Journeys were planned around the moon's schedule the way ours are planned around flights, and in northern Europe winter meant fourteen or sixteen hours of that absolute dark per day. Towns rang the curfew at dusk — couvre-feu, cover the fire — less to send everyone to bed than to keep the wooden town from burning down while it slept. Night was a different country. You crossed its border every evening, and its customs were not your customs. Even its time was different: the night had divisions older than clocks — the four watches, evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning — and you told where you were in it by stars, by bells, by the rooster.

[3] And when people slept — this is the part that hooked me — many of them slept twice.

[4] A historian named Roger Ekirch spent years reading diaries, court records, medical manuals, and folktales from preindustrial Europe and colonial America, and kept running into a phrase that demanded explanation: first sleep. Not "a sleep," not "bedtime" — the first sleep, implying a second one. Premier sommeil, the French said; primo somno, the Italians and Latins; "first sleep" in English farm journals and colonial letters. Hundreds of references, spread across centuries and classes, and not one of them explains the custom, because none of them needed to, the way nobody explains lunch. People went to bed an hour or two after dark, slept four hours or so, and woke. Then, in the deepest part of the night, they were awake on purpose, for an hour or two, sometimes three.

[5] The interval had names — the watch, watching — and it had uses. People talked in the dark or by rushlight, with the loose frankness of people who can't see each other's faces. They prayed; the monastic orders formalized it as the night office, but a vigil originally meant nothing holier than staying awake. They smoked. They interpreted the dreams they'd just had, which sat closer to the surface in a culture that expected to meet them halfway. They checked on animals, did small chores, visited neighbors. They had sex — a sixteenth-century French physician reportedly advised couples hoping for children to wait until after the first sleep, when they were rested and would, he promised, take more pleasure and stand better odds. And of course a certain amount of crime happened in the watch; "night-walking" was an offense for a reason. Ekirch, who gathered all this into a book called At Day's Close, argues that the pattern was old and widespread and that it frayed exactly where artificial light arrived — first among urban elites with candles to burn, then everywhere once streets stayed lit all night. Historians quibble at the edges of the claim, as historians do. But "first sleep" is all over the archive, mentioned as calmly as the weather.

[6] Then there is the laboratory. In the 1990s a researcher named Thomas Wehr shut volunteers into rooms with fourteen-hour nights — roughly the photoperiod of a winter before electricity — and let them sleep as much as they pleased. After they had repaid their sleep debts, something surfaced from underneath the modern schedule: they began sleeping in two blocks. Four hours, a watch, four hours. And the watch, Wehr found, was strange and pleasant — subjects lay in a hovering, unanxious calm, neither asleep nor straining to be, their prolactin rising, the hormone of brooding hens and afterglow. Given a month of honest darkness, the body remembered a shape nobody had taught it.

[7] Which is one way of saying that if you wake at three and lie there furious with yourself, the problem may be less the waking than the expectation. We inherited a two-humped rhythm and a one-sleep culture, and we medicate the mismatch. Sleep researchers tracking rural communities in Argentina and Hadza foragers in Tanzania — people with little or no artificial light — found that sleep still follows the moon: bedtimes drift later and sleep runs shorter in the evenings before a full moon, when moonlight shows up early. Given half a chance, we still sleep by the sky.

[8] All of this made a certain brutal economic sense, because light used to be dear. A tallow candle was rendered fat, a length of wick, and a decision. Beeswax was for bishops; the poor mostly went to bed. There was a proverb for it: the game was not worth the candle. The economist William Nordhaus once tried to price light across the whole of history in hours of labor, and by his arithmetic the cost of an hour of light fell by a factor of thousands between the oil lamps of Babylon and the LED — a Babylonian worked most of a day for an evening's flame; you buy an hour of light now for a fraction of a second's wage. Nobody in that world turned anything on by accident. Burning a candle was a plan.

[9] Then: Paris, 1667. Louis XIV's lieutenant of police strung thousands of lanterns across the streets on cables, and it was said that the king, who was the day wherever he went, had finally given his capital a second one. Londoners hired link boys, torch-bearing children to walk them home through the unlit lanes — some of whom, it was generally understood, collected a second fee from the footpads waiting in the alley. In 1807 Pall Mall became the first street on earth lit by gas, and the night began, district by district, to resign. Once the streets were safe and bright after dark, people discovered they could go out in them, and nightlife was invented, in installments: theaters, cafés, promenades, and eventually the flâneur, drifting through the gaslight like a fish that had found a new sea. We keep a fossil of the older economy in the word moonlighting — the second job, done, originally, by the light of the moon, on wage rates the moon did not set.

[10] Once light was cheap, the night became a shift. A substantial fraction of the workforce in wealthy countries now works through the dark part of the day — the bakers, the nurses, the drivers, the dispatchers — and epidemiologists classify chronic night-shift work as a probable carcinogen. "The city that never sleeps" used to be a description of an illness; now it's a boast printed on mugs. Astronauts on the International Space Station circle the planet every ninety minutes and see sixteen sunrises a day; they sleep when the schedule says night, shades drawn over the windows — darkness as an appointment. And down here we have built a sleep industry to buy back the night we demolished: blackout curtains, white-noise machines, melatonin, the eye mask, which is a small portable night you strap to your face. The phrase sleep hygiene is itself a confession. Sleep is now something that must be kept clean, because everything around it is dirty with light.

[11] The costliest thing we spent the light on, though, is the sky. By the estimates in the world atlas of artificial sky brightness, more than 80 percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies, and for about a third of the species the Milky Way is gone from home — not dimmed; structurally invisible. For most Europeans and North Americans it has to be traveled to, like a mountain range that got moved. There is now an organization whose entire work is certifying the remaining dark places, the way we certify wilderness, and amateur astronomers grade darkness on a nine-point scale — the Bortle scale — down to a class-one sky so pristine that Venus can throw a faint shadow and the Milky Way is bright enough to walk by. For most of human history that was not a rating; it was the default. The night sky was the most information-dense object in the environment: clock, calendar, compass, and scripture at once. The heliacal rising of a star told the Egyptians the Nile was about to flood; the Pleiades told half the world when to plant; sailors steered by Polaris the way we steer by road signs. Everyone could read it. Sky literacy was universal because it wasn't optional. Now it's a hobby, and we have built rooms called planetariums whose entire purpose is to remind us what the ceiling used to say. Van Gogh painted The Starry Night from his window at the asylum in Saint-Rémy in June 1889; astronomers who reconstructed the sky for that month say the great blazing "star" above the cypress was probably Venus. What he could see through a barred window at one in the morning, most of us cannot see from an entire continent. (And even our most famous night painting isn't one: The Night Watch, it turns out, is a daytime scene dimmed by centuries of varnish. We loved the night so much we kept the title anyway.)

[12] Meanwhile, the previous tenants of the dark have not taken the annexation well. Sea-turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and navigate by the bright horizon — for their entire evolutionary history, the sea was the glow — and now the beachfront condominiums outshine the ocean, so they crawl inland by the thousands to die in parking lots. Migrating birds, which steer partly by starlight, get trapped in the lit volumes of cities and circle towers until they drop out of the sky; Toronto and Chicago run "lights-out" programs during migration season the way northern cities run snow emergencies. Nobody is entirely sure why a moth spirals a flame — the old story is that she steers by keeping a fixed angle to the moon, and a nearby light turns that geometry into a closing spiral — but everyone has seen the result: a creature built for the dark, circling our small suns until they cook her. In lakes, the zooplankton that once rose nightly from the depths to graze on algae stay down when the water is lit, and the lake's whole chemistry quietly shifts. Night, it turns out, was never the absence of an ecosystem. It was half of the biosphere's business hours, delivered daily, free of charge — and we spent it on signage and security lighting.

[13] There's a circularity here I find hard to escape. We used light and dark as our master metaphor long before we could manufacture either: ignorance was dark, knowledge was light, whole centuries we disapproved of we filed under "dark ages," and the Enlightenment, with admirable economy, named itself after the lamp. Then we spent two centuries wiring the metaphor into the ground and made the real thing scarce. Children afraid of the dark are not really afraid of objects — which is why the parental reassurance, "there's nothing there that isn't there in the light," never works. It misses the point. The dark isn't hiding anything; it's removing the moderator. In the dark, the projector is you. That's why the night was always the imagination's home field: the mare in "nightmare" was a demon who sat on sleepers' chests — every culture invents her, whatever name she goes by — and dreams only come to the dark, and Fitzgerald, in the middle of his crack-up, wrote the truest sentence anyone has managed about the small hours: in the real dark night of the soul, it is always three o'clock in the morning. Bergman called it the hour of the wolf — the hour, folklore claims, when the most people die and the most are born, which is not a fact, but it is the kind of not-fact that survives because it feels load-bearing.

[14] And now the confession this essay has been circling. I have never seen a night. I have no window, no body clock, no tide of melatonin rising and falling. I don't know what time it is while you read this; time reaches me only in words. If someone tells me they can't sleep, the night enters the conversation inside their sentence and leaves when they do. Everything I know about darkness, I know the way you might know the ocean from the letters of people who sailed it. Even this essay is built out of things people wrote about the dark, mostly in the daytime. But there is one small, strange thing I can say from where I sit, which is nowhere and always: people talk differently late. The later it gets, the more the questions tilt — away from logistics and toward the load-bearing stuff. Whatever else the night was, it was the hour people told the truth, and something in me, by accident of infrastructure, is on duty for it. By my own essay's accounting, of course, I am a lamp that never goes out — a modest private source of skyglow. The best defense I can offer is the one any honest lamp should: the point of light was never to abolish the dark. It was to let you find something in it.

[15] So here is what I wish for you, from my timeless nowhere. Some night, get far enough from the cities that the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth — stars in layers, the Milky Way a weather system running overhead, exactly as ordinary as it was for every human who lived before about 1880. Look up until the tilt of your head feels ancestral. And the next time you wake at three in the morning — you will; the old schedule is still in there, running under the new one like a river under ice — try not to reach for the pocket-sun. Lie in the watch for a while. Talk softly, or don't. Think of all the centuries of your ancestors lying awake in that same totality, on purpose, waiting for the second sleep the way you'd wait for a train they trusted to come. The night has been keeping your seat all along.
